t: Introduction: topic, aim and plan
n: In this session we will examine the liability of the medical worker in three areas. The first is disciplinary liability: violating labour discipline is a disciplinary offence, and the employer may hold the employee to disciplinary liability. The second is administrative liability: it arises for an administrative offence, and for professional offences of medical workers a fine is most often applied. The third is civil-law liability, that is, compensation for the harm caused. Remember: being held to another liability does not release one from compensating for harm. The plan is as follows: first labour legislation and disciplinary penalties, then administrative liability, and finally questions of compensation for harm.

t: Main content of labour legislation
n: We begin with the main content of labour legislation. Under Article 37 of the Constitution, a citizen has the right to work, to freely choose a job, to work under fair conditions and to protection against unemployment. The main source in regulating labour relations in line with the principles of a market economy is the Labour Code. Labour law regulates the relations of the employee and the employer on the basis of the employment contract. The law sets out the procedure for establishing, changing and terminating relations. The law also determines the volume of work, wages, internal order, discipline, occupational safety and disputes.

t: Specific nature of labour relations
n: The specific nature of labour relations is that by four features they differ from other legal relations, for example from civil law. Feature A: the relation arises in production. Feature B: the employee is a member of a collective and has rights and duties. Feature C: labour is a paid relation. Feature D: labour is personal and is performed in a definite profession or post. One more important rule: forced labour, that is, compelling a person to work under threat of punishment, is prohibited. Military or alternative service, a state of emergency, a court sentence: in such cases certain work is not considered forced labour.

t: Rights of the employee and the employer
n: Now the rights of the employee and the employer. The employee's rights are given in Article 16 of the Labour Code, that is, the LC: these are wages, rest and safe conditions. The employer concludes and terminates contracts and also demands full performance of the work; this is stated in Article 17 of the LC. The employee may defend his rights in court and receive qualified legal aid. That is, the employee's rights cover wages, rest, safe conditions and judicial protection, while the employer's rights consist in concluding and terminating the contract and demanding full performance of the work.

t: Duties of the employee and the employer
n: Now the duties. Under Article 176 of the LC, the employee performs his duties honestly, observes discipline and safety engineering, and looks after property. The employer's duties are in Article 177 of the LC: he organises the work, creates the conditions stipulated in the contract and observes occupational safety. In addition, there is a prohibition: the employer cannot demand work that is not part of the employee's duties. Nor is he entitled to demand work that harms life or honour. This prohibition protects the employee from the employer's unfounded demands.

t: Employment contract and hiring
n: The employment contract and the hiring procedure, step by step. First of all, documents are handed over: passport, work record book, military document and diploma; part-time workers provide a certificate. The contract states the place of work, the duty, the start time and the pay. If no term is stated, the contract is considered to be for an indefinite period. Probation does not exceed three months, and for pregnant women and women with children under three years of age probation is not set. During probation the contract may be terminated with 3 days' written notice. If the employee continues to work after the probation period has passed, the contract remains in force.

t: Collective agreement
n: A collective agreement is a normative document regulating labour, socio-economic and professional relations between the employer and the employees at an enterprise. Its principles: compliance with the law, competence, freedom of choice and discussion, voluntariness, ensuring performance, inspection and inevitable liability. The parties are the trade union or an authorised body and the employer. Terms more favourable than those in the law, such as additional leave, may be included. The procedure is as follows: the draft is first discussed with the employees and then put to a general meeting. The term is set by the parties, and when it ends the agreement remains in force until a new one is concluded.

t: Quick questions: basics of the employment contract
n: Let us consider quick questions on the basics of the employment contract. First question: what if no term is stated in the contract? Answer: it is considered concluded for an indefinite period, and it cannot be re-concluded for a definite period without the employee's consent. Second question: how long does probation last? Answer: not more than three months, and it is not set for a pregnant woman or a woman with a child under three years of age. Third question: how many days in advance is notice given to terminate the contract during probation? Answer: three days, in writing. Fourth question: can the employer demand work that is not part of the duties? Answer: no; nor can he demand work that is contrary to law or dangerous to life and health.

t: Part-time work, several professions and substitution
n: The concepts of part-time work, several professions and substitution. Working in several professions is possible only when the established volume of work has been performed at the main place and in the main time. Attention: part-time work, several professions and substitution are not the same thing; distinguish them by the place and time of work. In internal part-time work, the employee in his free time does paid work in his own institution, for example extra work in his own hospital. In external part-time work, he works in his free time in another institution. In working in several professions, an additional, different post is held in the same institution. In substitution, the work of a temporarily absent employee is also performed. A head is permitted to work as a doctor, and a doctor as a mid-level medical worker.

t: Working time and occupational safety
n: Working time and occupational safety. Normal working time does not exceed 40 hours per week, and for medical workers it is shortened to 36 hours. Within occupational safety, the employer organises preliminary and periodic medical examinations. The employee cannot refuse this examination. The employee does not pay the cost of the examination. If the employee's health has deteriorated, he may ask for an extraordinary examination. Remember: normal working time is 40 hours, for medical workers up to 36 hours, and the cost of the examination does not fall on the employee.

t: Termination of the employment contract: the employee's initiative
n: The general grounds for terminating an employment contract are: agreement, the initiative of one party, expiry of the term and circumstances beyond the parties' will. Now we will look at the stages of termination on the employee's initiative. At the first stage, the employee submits a written application. The second stage is the warning: the employee can terminate an open-ended or fixed-term contract by giving two weeks' written notice. Third stage: until the term expires, the application can be withdrawn. At the fourth stage, work stops when the term has passed. At the fifth stage, the record book is issued and final settlement is made. If the contract is not terminated even after the notice period has ended, the application loses force.

t: Employer's initiative: grounds and notice
n: Termination on the employer's initiative has two conditions: a ground set out in the Code, and compliance with all formal requirements, that is, notice and an offer of other work. Ground and notice period: for staff reduction or liquidation of the enterprise, at least two months in advance; for insufficient qualification or on grounds of health, at least two weeks in advance; for systematic violation and a single gross violation, three days in advance or compensation. Systematic violation means repeated misconduct within one year after the previous penalty. The contract cannot be terminated during temporary incapacity for work or leave; the exception is liquidation of the enterprise.

t: Disciplinary penalties and the procedure for applying them
n: Types of disciplinary penalty: reprimand, a fine of up to 30% of the average monthly wage, and termination of the employment contract. Before the penalty, a written explanation is requested. If the employee refuses to give one, the penalty can still be applied. One penalty is imposed for each violation, and it is announced by order. The limits are as follows: the fine is usually up to 30%, the time limit for applying the penalty is 1 month, the ultimate limit is 6 months, with an audit 2 years, and the penalty remains in effect for 1 year. That is, these time limits must be clearly distinguished.

t: Case analysis: disciplinary penalty and dismissal
n: Case analysis. Situation: a doctor on duty violated the internal labour regulations, and the manager discovered it. Then the employee went on annual leave. Question: within what period is the penalty applied? Answer: within one month of the offence being discovered; the time of leave or illness is not counted in this period. A written explanation is required from the employee. To terminate the contract, systematic violation is needed, that is, repeated misconduct within a year after the previous penalty; a single gross violation is also a ground. Attention, there is a risk of error: the time limit for applying the penalty is 1 month, while the period in which the penalty remains in effect is 1 year. Do not confuse them.

t: Administrative legislation and the concept of offence
n: Administrative legislation is a body of legal documents regulating public relations in state administration and other fields. It sets rules such as sanitary and licensing rules, and provides for liability for violating them and the procedure for imposing penalties. The Constitution, together with the rights of citizens, also establishes the equality of their duties; failure to perform a duty becomes grounds for measures provided by law. An administrative offence is a culpable action or omission that infringes rights, property, public order and the natural environment. It lacks the feature of social danger.

t: Forms of fault: intent and negligence
n: Fault takes two forms: intent and negligence. In committing an act intentionally, the person knows his action is unlawful, foresees the consequence, and desires it or consciously allows it. In negligence, however, the person does not desire the consequence. Two cases are possible here. The first is frivolity: the person foresaw the consequence but counted on preventing it. The second: the person should and could have foreseen the consequence, but did not foresee it. The difference is that in intent the consequence is desired or consciously accepted.

t: Difference between an administrative offence and a crime
n: The difference between an administrative offence and a crime. An administrative offence does not carry signs of danger to society, so criminal liability does not arise; it is an unlawful, culpable act that brings administrative liability. A crime, however, has signs of social danger, and criminal liability arises. Depending on the significance, the gravity of the consequence and the number of acts committed, some administrative offences may be assessed as a crime. Attention: violating sanitary or anti-epidemic rules can become a crime. That is, with a grave consequence an administrative act may take on the character of a crime.

t: Circumstances excluding liability
n: Circumstances excluding liability. The first is extreme necessity: if the danger cannot be averted by other measures and the harm caused is less than the harm prevented, the action is not an offence. The second is age: persons who had not reached sixteen years at the time of the offence are not held to administrative liability. The third: if the offence is minor, the body considering the case, that is, the official, may release the person from liability and limit itself to a warning. Attention: in civil legislation, extreme necessity does not automatically release from compensating for harm; the harm, as a rule, is paid by the person who caused it.

t: Quick questions: features of an administrative offence
n: Quick questions on the features of an administrative offence. First question: what is an administrative offence? Answer: an unlawful, culpable, that is, intentional or negligent, action or omission. Second question: how do intent and negligence differ? Answer: in intent, the person desires the harmful consequence or consciously allows it. Third question, with attention here: an administrative offence is not a crime. How do they differ? Answer: an administrative act has no signs of danger to society. Fourth question: from what age does liability arise? Answer: persons who had not reached 16 at the time of committing the offence are not held to administrative liability.

t: Types of administrative penalty
n: Types of administrative penalty. Article 23 of the Code of Administrative Liability, that is, the CAL, lists five punitive measures: fine, compensated seizure, confiscation, deprivation of a special right, and administrative detention. A penalty is either principal, or principal and additional; seizure and confiscation are applied in both forms. Attention: in seizure, the item is sold and the money returned to the owner; in confiscation, no payment is made. Remember this difference well, because it is exactly what is asked in the examination.

t: Amounts of fines
n: Amounts of fines. A fine is calculated from the minimum monthly wage; for a continuing offence, the amount at the time of discovery is the basis. A fine is the recovery of money in favour of the state, and its amount differs for a citizen and an official. For a citizen the minimum is 1/50 of the wage, the maximum is 5 times, in exceptional cases up to 100 times, and under a local decision up to 3 times. For an official the minimum is 1/10 of the wage, the maximum is 10 times, in exceptional cases up to 150 times, and under a local decision up to 5 times. Decisions of local authorities set a fine in the fight for public order, in natural disasters and in epidemics.

t: Seizure, confiscation and time limits for penalty
n: Seizure, confiscation and time limits for the penalty. In compensated seizure, the item that was the instrument or object of the offence is taken by force and sold, and the proceeds, less costs, are given to the former owner. In confiscation, the item passes without payment into state ownership; the decision is made by the administrative judge of the district or city court, and by tax and customs bodies. Both measures may be a principal or an additional penalty and may be applied in private medical or pharmaceutical practice. Time limit: the penalty may not be imposed later than two months from the day of the offence or, if it is continuing, from the day it was discovered. If a criminal case is refused or terminated, one month from the day of the decision.

t: Bodies considering the case, and the record
n: Who considers the case and how the record is drawn up. The case is considered by a judge, a commercial court, administrative commissions, internal affairs bodies and inspectorates. The procedure is this: first, a violation of the rules is identified in an inspection. Then a record is drawn up, in which the date, place, essence of the offence, regulatory document, witnesses and written explanation are entered. The record is signed by the person who drew it up, the offender, the witness and the victim. If someone refuses to sign, this is entered in the record. Then the case is considered by the judge, commission or inspection body.

t: Rights of the person being held liable
n: The rights of the person being held liable. Under Article 294 of the CAL, the person gets acquainted with the case materials, gives explanations, presents evidence and files requests. These rights must be explained to him when the record is drawn up. He also has the right to the help of a lawyer, to speak in his native language, to an interpreter's services and to appeal the decision. The case is usually considered with the person present; if he has been notified and has made no request for postponement, it may be considered without him. In detention, confiscation and seizure, attendance is mandatory. The person who has suffered harm is the victim and has the same rights as the accused. If special knowledge is required, an expert examination is ordered.

t: Offences infringing citizens' rights
n: Offences infringing citizens' rights. The Code of Administrative Liability, that is, the CAL, lists separately acts infringing the rights and freedoms of citizens. They are: slander, Article 40; insult, Article 41; the state language, Article 42; citizens' appeals, Article 43; violation of the labour law, Article 49; administrative coercion to work, Article 51. These offences relate more to the activity not of medical workers but of heads of medical institutions. Attention, there is a risk of error: an ordinary medical worker and the head of an institution are not the same. In these articles the subject is most often the head.

t: Offences in the field of health care
n: Offences in the field of health care. Offences concerning public health are set out in Chapter VI of the CAL; the subject may also be a medical worker. Articles 52-56 cover questions of injury, sanitation, epidemics and radiation. Articles 57-59 relate to AIDS, that is, acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, and to venereal diseases: concealing the source and refusing examination. Articles 164, 176 and others relate to private practice. Articles 199 and 215 on the order of administration include a false call to the ambulance service. State medical workers who work on a paid basis and on a self-financing basis may also be held liable.

t: Case analysis: medical worker and administrative liability
n: Case analysis. Situation: in a medical institution the rules of anti-epidemic control were violated; this relates to Article 54 of the CAL. The authorised official drew up a record. The record states the date, place, the essence of the offence, the regulatory document and the offender's written explanation, and the person is told his rights. The case is considered by authorised bodies such as State Sanitary Supervision. The principal punishment is, as a rule, a fine; for a citizen from 1/50 to 5 times the minimum monthly wage. Question: how does the amount of the fine for an official differ from that for a citizen? How may the act be assessed if the consequence is grave?

t: Civil law and tort liability
n: Civil law regulates the property and related non-property relations of citizens and organisations. Subjects: the natural person, the legal entity and the state. To be a subject, legal capacity is needed, that is, the ability to have rights and duties, and capacity to act, that is, the ability, by one's own actions, to acquire rights and answer for them. Attention: tort liability and contractual liability are not the same thing. In tort, general objective criteria apply; in contract, only breach of the contract. Doctors more often encounter tort. Harm is of two kinds: actual damage, that is, the costs of treatment and medicines, and lost profit, that is, wages or income the patient did not receive.

t: Conditions for liability for harm to arise
n: For liability for harm to arise, four conditions must be present together. The first is the fact that harm was caused. The second is an unlawful action. The third is a causal link. The fourth is the fault of the person who caused the harm. Only when these conditions are present does liability arise. Fault takes two forms: intent or negligence, that is, carelessness and overconfidence. Care that does not comply with the standard, the contract or ordinary requirements is considered improper medical care.

t: Personal non-property rights and the principle of tort
n: The principle of tort is that one person's causing harm to another itself gives rise to the obligation to compensate. In contractual liability, an unlawful action means only a breach of the contract's requirements; its extent should not be less than in tort. Now the personal non-property rights: life and health, honour and dignity, personal inviolability, business reputation, private life and family secrecy. Among the ways of protecting civil rights are compensation for losses and compensation for moral harm; this is stated in Article 15 of the Civil Code.

t: Harm from defects in goods, work and services (Civil Code 1017-1020)
n: Harm from defects in goods, work and services is regulated by Articles 1017-1020 of the Civil Code. If a design, formulation or other defect, or incorrect or insufficient information, causes harm to life, health or property, this harm is compensated; this is Civil Code 1017. The harm is compensated by the seller or manufacturer, that is, the performer, regardless of whether there was a contract. Harm from a defect in a product is compensated, at the victim's choice, by the seller or manufacturer, for example for a medicine or equipment; harm from a defect in a service is compensated by the performer; this is Civil Code 1018. If force majeure or violation of the rules by the consumer is proved, the responsible person is released; this is Civil Code 1020.

t: Cases of innocence and the presumption of fault
n: The presumption of fault means that fault is presumed. The victim does not have to prove fault and the unlawfulness of the action; the person who caused the harm proves his own innocence. So if the patient accuses the doctor, the doctor is considered guilty until he proves that his action is lawful and free of fault. As a rule, the employee is found not guilty in three cases: force majeure; harm caused at the patient's request or with his consent; gross negligence of the patient himself. In such a dispute, medical records are of particular importance: the original, the completeness of the daily notes and the absence of corrections.

t: Quick questions: civil liability
n: Quick questions on civil liability. First question: which liability more often arises in a professional offence of a medical worker, tort or contractual? Second question: the patient accuses the doctor; who must prove the doctor's innocence, and why? Third question: with which four conditions present together does liability for harm arise? Fourth question: the doctor has been held to disciplinary, administrative or criminal liability; does this release him from compensating for harm? Think, and answer on the basis of the rules of the previous slides.

t: Compensation for harm: recourse, insurance, limitation period
n: The procedure for compensating harm. The institution compensates harm caused by an employee in the course of his duties. The institution that has paid may, by way of recourse, demand this sum from the employee, but in practice this is rare. If liability is insured and the insurance sum does not cover the harm completely, the insured person himself pays the difference. Attention: in criminal legislation extreme necessity removes liability, but in civil law it does not release from compensating for harm. The general limitation period is three years; it runs from the day the person learned, or should have learned, of the violation of his right.

t: Provision of medical services under a contract
n: Provision of medical services under a contract. A contract is an agreement to establish, change or terminate rights and duties. In medical services a paid contract is concluded: the performer provides the service, and the customer pays. The consequences depend on fault. If the performer carried out the service incorrectly, he compensates the harm in full, but not more than twice the price of the service. If performance is impossible through the customer's fault, the price of the service is paid in full. If the parties are not at fault and the service was not performed, the customer pays the performer's costs.

t: Moral harm and consumer rights
n: Moral harm is physical and moral suffering resulting from an infringement of personal non-property rights. Its amount is determined by the court, taking into account reasonableness and fairness; it is paid independently of property damage. Under Article 22 of the law, the payment for moral harm is determined by the court. Consumer rights: information, choice, safety and compensation. The patient is considered the consumer, and the medical worker and the institution the performer. Under Article 1126 of the Civil Code, the will of an in-patient is certified by the chief physician.

t: Will of a patient (Civil Code 1126)
n: The will of a patient is regulated by Article 1126 of the Civil Code. The wills of citizens receiving treatment in a hospital, military hospital or other in-patient facility, or living in a home for the elderly and disabled, are certified in a special way. Those who certify: the chief physician, the deputy for treatment or the duty doctor; the head of the military hospital; the director or chief physician of a home for the elderly and disabled. A will certified in this way is equated with a notarised one. The medical worker, along with compensation for material and moral harm, may also encounter cases of witnessing wills.

t: Compensation for moral harm: court criteria
n: The court criteria for compensating moral harm. Moral harm is physical and moral suffering resulting from an infringement of personal non-property rights or intangible benefits; this is Civil Code 1021. The court determines the amount reasonably and fairly, according to the nature of the suffering, the details of the circumstances, the characteristics of the victim and the degree of fault; this is Civil Code 1022. Moral harm is compensated irrespective of the property damage that must be paid. Rudeness towards the patient, disrespect and disclosure of medical confidentiality may be grounds for compensating moral harm even when there is no material damage. Payment is made in money.

t: Case analysis: harm to a patient and compensation
n: Case analysis. Situation, a teaching example: proper care was not given to a patient, and harm was done to his health. He claims treatment costs and compensation for moral harm. If an employee caused harm in the course of his official duties, the institution compensates. The institution can then demand the sum paid back from the employee; this is recourse. Fault is presumed: the patient does not have to prove it. The employee or the institution proves innocence, for example by the completeness of the documents. The court determines the amount of moral harm by the nature of the suffering and the degree of fault; it is paid irrespective of property damage.

t: Conclusion and review questions
n: Let us summarise. Disciplinary liability: a reprimand, a fine of up to 30 per cent of the average monthly wage, or termination of the contract; the penalty remains in effect for one year. Administrative liability: most often a fine; persons under 16 are not liable, and the penalty is usually imposed within two months. Civil liability consists in compensating harm, and being held to another liability does not release one from compensating for harm. Attention: an administrative fine is recovered in favour of the state, while compensation for harm restores the victim's right. They do not replace each other. As review questions, try to explain for yourself the difference between these three liabilities.
